title: ayam atma brahma — a week each
hook: ayam atma brahma — a week each
carry: ayam atma brahma — a week each
tomorrow: you keep promising to change a habit. where does change start?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed tat tvam asi: one line heard as one awareness, as Brahman with its body, and as a real difference. The great sayings get about a week each. Here comes the next, and it trades that for this.

On a video call, someone holds a thing right up to the camera: this one. Not the one on the shelf over there. This. Tat, that, pointed across a distance. Today's saying trades it for ayam, this: the near one, within reach. It comes from the Mandukya, a short Upanishad about Om, and it starts close to home.
screen: `HELD UP TO THE CAMERA.` → `NOT THAT ONE. THIS ONE.` → `AYAM: THE NEAR WORD.`

segments.voice: Near its start, the Mandukya sets three short sentences side by side. In paraphrase: all this is Brahman. This self is Brahman. This self has four quarters. The middle one is the great saying: ayam atma brahma. Look at how they fit. The first is about everything at once: all this. The second narrows to one pointing word, ayam, this, and lands it on the self. The third turns toward looking: if this self is Brahman, here's how to see it, in quarters. The quarters come in the verses that follow, and the days ahead take some of them in turn. For now, stay with the pointing. Ayam is the word for what's near: the cup in your hand, not the hill on the horizon. That gives the saying its feel. It doesn't say a self somewhere is Brahman. It says this one, the one breathing while these words go by. The sayings so far each brought a word: prajnanam brahma named the knowing, aham brahmasmi said I, tat tvam asi said you. Ayam atma brahma points, and leaves the looking to the one who hears it.
screen: `ALL THIS IS BRAHMAN.` · `THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.` · `FOUR QUARTERS, TO SEE IT BY.` · then, large: `THIS ONE. RIGHT HERE.`

segments.voice: Look at something far away, a window or the wall across the room, and notice the word that fits it: that. Then rest one hand on your chest and feel it rise and fall. With each rise, let the other word come: this.
Ayam atma brahma: this self is Brahman, with ayam, this, pointing at the self right here.
Your line: ayam atma brahma, a week each, and this week belongs to this self, right here. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Mandukya Upanishad is studied as a teaching on Om, and ayam atma brahma, from its second verse, is taught as one of the great sayings of the Upanishads.

chat.meaning: In the Mandukya, ayam is the near word, this: this self is Brahman, not a self somewhere far off.
